question: Which lung volume describes the gas remaining after maximal expiration?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the lung volumes and capacities (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Residual volume remaining after maximal expiration
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines residual volume as the gas left after maximal expiration.

options.text: Tidal volume measured during quiet resting breathing
options.rationale: Wrong because tidal volume is the air moved with each normal breath; if maximal expiration occurred this would not be tidal volume.

options.text: Expiratory reserve volume below normal tidal expiration
options.rationale: Wrong because expiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be expired after a normal tidal expiration, not the volume remaining after maximal expiration.

options.text: Inspiratory reserve volume above normal tidal inspiration
options.rationale: Wrong because inspiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be inspired above tidal volume, not the residual gas after maximal expiration.

options.text: Functional residual capacity at equilibrium after tidal expiration
options.rationale: Wrong because functional residual capacity includes residual volume plus expiratory reserve volume and is the equilibrium volume after tidal expiration, not the single residual volume alone.

question: A patient breathes room air at sea level. Which equation component most directly determines alveolar oxygen partial pressure?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the factors regulating O2 and CO2 alveolar pressures (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Fractional inspired oxygen concentration in inspired gas
options.rationale: Correct because the alveolar gas equation shows PAO2 depends directly on the inspired oxygen fraction as taught in the lecture.

options.text: Pulmonary capillary blood hemoglobin concentration value
options.rationale: Wrong because hemoglobin concentration affects oxygen content but not the alveolar PO2 in the alveolar gas equation; a change in hemoglobin would not directly change PAO2.

options.text: Alveolar surface area available for diffusion across membrane
options.rationale: Wrong because surface area affects diffusion rate and transfer to blood but does not directly set alveolar PO2 in the alveolar gas equation.

options.text: Systemic arterial oxygen content measured after gas exchange
options.rationale: Wrong because arterial oxygen content reflects postalveolar exchange and is influenced by PAO2 but does not itself determine PAO2.

options.text: Hemoglobin oxygen affinity as reflected by dissociation curve
options.rationale: Wrong because hemoglobin affinity alters oxygen binding and content but does not directly determine alveolar PO2 according to the alveolar gas equation.

question: Which factor most directly lowers alveolar PACO2 when metabolic rate is constant?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the factors regulating O2 and CO2 alveolar pressures (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increase in alveolar ventilation per minute
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states PACO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation when metabolic rate is constant.

options.text: Increase in inspired oxygen fraction without ventilation change
options.rationale: Wrong because increasing inspired oxygen raises PAO2 but does not directly lower PACO2 unless ventilation changes.

options.text: Increase in hemoglobin concentration in pulmonary blood
options.rationale: Wrong because hemoglobin concentration affects oxygen content but does not directly change alveolar CO2 partial pressure.

options.text: Decrease in atmospheric barometric pressure at altitude
options.rationale: Wrong because lower barometric pressure reduces PAO2 but does not directly reduce PACO2 unless ventilation or metabolism change.

options.text: Increase in diffusion surface area of alveolar membrane
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion area affects gas transfer efficiency but PACO2 is set primarily by ventilation relative to metabolism.

question: Which structural change most increases airway resistance according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Decrease in airway radius due to smooth muscle constriction
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes airway radius as the primary determinant of resistance and bronchoconstriction reduces radius.

options.text: Loss of alveolar elastic recoil increasing radial traction
options.rationale: Wrong because loss of elastic recoil, as in emphysema, tends to reduce radial traction and increase airway collapse but the phrase increasing radial traction is incorrect for that pathology.

options.text: Increase in cartilaginous support of small bronchioles
options.rationale: Wrong because increased cartilage would stabilize airways and lower resistance rather than increase it.

options.text: Thickening of alveolar walls with increased compliance
options.rationale: Wrong because alveolar wall thickening reduces compliance and affects diffusion but does not directly increase airway resistance via radius change.

options.text: Enhanced parasympathetic vagal inhibition of mucus secretion
options.rationale: Wrong because parasympathetic activity increases bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion; inhibition of mucus secretion would not increase resistance.

question: A spirometry tracing shows FEV1/FVC ratio less than 70 percent. Which category best fits this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the types of compliance depending on the lung diseases (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Obstructive pulmonary disease pattern with airflow limitation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states obstructive diseases produce a markedly reduced FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio below 70 percent.

options.text: Restrictive pulmonary disease pattern with reduced lung volumes
options.rationale: Wrong because restrictive disease typically preserves or increases FEV1/FVC ratio while reducing absolute volumes.

options.text: Normal pulmonary function with age related decline
options.rationale: Wrong because a ratio below 70 percent indicates pathological obstruction rather than normal aging alone.

options.text: Upper airway fixed obstruction causing flow limitation
options.rationale: Wrong because fixed upper airway obstruction produces a different flow-volume loop pattern and does not typically present solely as low FEV1/FVC ratio.

options.text: Primary pulmonary vascular disease without airway involvement
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary vascular disease affects perfusion and pressures rather than producing a low FEV1/FVC ratio from airway obstruction.

question: Which histologic airway layer is absent in alveoli and contributes to gas exchange efficiency?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the lung volumes and capacities (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Ciliated epithelial cells absent in alveolar lining
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes alveoli lack cilia, which contributes to their thin walls optimized for diffusion.

options.text: Type II pneumocytes absent in alveolar lining
options.rationale: Wrong because type II pneumocytes are present in alveoli and produce surfactant and serve as progenitors for type I cells.

options.text: Alveolar macrophages absent in alveolar lining
options.rationale: Wrong because alveolar macrophages are present and provide immune protection within alveoli.

options.text: Smooth muscle cells absent in alveolar lining
options.rationale: Wrong because while smooth muscle is absent in alveoli, the lecture specifically highlights absence of cilia as a distinguishing histologic feature.

options.text: Cartilage absent in alveolar lining and small airways
options.rationale: Wrong because cartilage is absent in bronchioles and alveoli but the key histologic absence emphasized for alveoli is cilia rather than cartilage.

question: A patient with emphysema has loss of alveolar walls. Which compliance change is expected?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the types of compliance depending on the lung diseases (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increased lung compliance due to loss of elastic fibers
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains emphysema destroys elastic fibers and increases compliance making lungs easier to inflate but harder to recoil.

options.text: Decreased lung compliance due to fibrotic replacement
options.rationale: Wrong because fibrotic diseases decrease compliance, which is characteristic of restrictive rather than emphysematous pathology.

options.text: Unchanged compliance with increased airway resistance only
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema alters compliance by destroying alveolar walls and elastic tissue; compliance does not remain unchanged.

options.text: Decreased compliance due to surfactant deficiency
options.rationale: Wrong because surfactant deficiency reduces compliance but is not the mechanism in emphysema where elastic fiber loss increases compliance.

options.text: Variable compliance with no predictable directional change
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture specifies emphysema produces increased compliance, so the change is predictable rather than variable.

question: Which mechanism best explains hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated lung regions?
cited_learning_objective: Define the category of hypoxic vasoconstriction (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Precapillary vasoconstriction diverting blood from hypoxic alveoli
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes hypoxic vasoconstriction as precapillary constriction that redirects blood away from poorly ventilated regions.

options.text: Postcapillary venoconstriction increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture specifies precapillary constriction as the mechanism rather than postcapillary venoconstriction.

options.text: Systemic vasodilation increasing pulmonary blood flow to hypoxic areas
options.rationale: Wrong because systemic vasodilation would not selectively divert pulmonary blood away from hypoxic alveoli and contradicts the described pulmonary response.

options.text: Endothelial nitric oxide release causing local vasodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because nitric oxide mediated vasodilation opposes vasoconstriction and is not the mechanism of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction described in the lecture.

options.text: Increased sympathetic tone causing global pulmonary vasodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because sympathetic-mediated vasodilation is not the localized precapillary constriction mechanism that diverts blood from hypoxic regions.

question: A COPD patient with chronic hypoventilation receives high supplemental oxygen. What risk is emphasized by the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the main mechanisms of respiratory regulation (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Loss of peripheral hypoxic drive causing hypoventilation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture warns that in chronic CO2 retainers ventilation may depend on low PO2 drive and supplemental oxygen can remove that drive leading to hypoventilation.

options.text: Immediate reversal of pulmonary hypertension with oxygen therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because while oxygen can reduce hypoxic vasoconstriction, it does not immediately reverse established pulmonary hypertension in chronic disease as implied.

options.text: Increased central chemoreceptor sensitivity to carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic CO2 retention actually blunts central chemoreceptor sensitivity rather than increasing it.

options.text: Enhanced mucociliary clearance improving ventilation uniformly
options.rationale: Wrong because supplemental oxygen does not directly enhance mucociliary clearance and this is not the risk highlighted in the lecture.

options.text: Acute bronchoconstriction due to oxygen induced airway irritation
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen therapy does not typically cause acute bronchoconstriction and this is not the mechanism discussed in the lecture.

question: Which change in a flow-volume loop is most characteristic of fixed upper airway stenosis?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Flattening of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes fixed upper airway obstruction as producing loss of effort-dependent and independent portions leading to flattened inspiratory and expiratory limbs.

options.text: Scooped expiratory downslope typical of peripheral obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because the scooped expiratory pattern is characteristic of obstructive peripheral airway disease, not fixed upper airway stenosis.

options.text: High peak flow with low total lung volumes
options.rationale: Wrong because high peak flow with low volumes is more consistent with restrictive disease rather than fixed upper airway stenosis.

options.text: Normal loop with reduced residual volume only
options.rationale: Wrong because fixed upper airway stenosis alters the shape of the loop rather than producing an otherwise normal loop with isolated residual volume change.

options.text: Increased expiratory flow at all lung volumes
options.rationale: Wrong because fixed stenosis reduces peak flow and flattens limbs rather than increasing expiratory flow.

question: Which cell type produces surfactant and serves as progenitor for type I pneumocytes?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the lung volumes and capacities (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Type II pneumocytes producing surfactant and regenerating
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states type II pneumocytes produce surfactant and can differentiate into type I cells during regeneration.

options.text: Type I pneumocytes thin cells covering most surface
options.rationale: Wrong because type I pneumocytes are thin and cover most surface but do not produce surfactant or serve as progenitors.

options.text: Alveolar macrophages providing immune defense in alveoli
options.rationale: Wrong because alveolar macrophages provide protection but do not produce surfactant or regenerate type I cells.

options.text: Fibroblasts secreting type IV collagen in interstitium
options.rationale: Wrong because fibroblasts secrete collagen and contribute to interstitial structure but are not surfactant producers or progenitors for pneumocytes.

options.text: Bronchiolar Clara cells secreting club cell secretions
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchiolar club cells secrete protective proteins in bronchioles but are not the alveolar type II cells described in the lecture.

question: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis will most likely have which compliance curve shift?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the types of compliance depending on the lung diseases (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Downward and rightward shift indicating decreased compliance
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture indicates fibrosis reduces compliance so more negative intrapleural pressure is needed to achieve the same volume.

options.text: Upward and leftward shift indicating increased compliance
options.rationale: Wrong because increased compliance is seen in emphysema, not in fibrotic restrictive disease.

options.text: No shift with only increased airway resistance present
options.rationale: Wrong because fibrosis changes elastic properties and thus shifts the compliance curve rather than leaving it unchanged.

options.text: Oscillating shift depending on respiratory rate alone
options.rationale: Wrong because compliance changes are structural and not simply oscillatory with respiratory rate.

options.text: Initial increase then late decrease in compliance curve
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture describes a consistent decrease in compliance with fibrosis rather than a biphasic pattern.

question: Which local mediator listed in the lecture directly causes bronchoconstriction?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Histamine released during allergic inflammation causing constriction
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists histamine as a local factor that constricts bronchioles.

options.text: Norepinephrine activating beta two receptors causing dilation
options.rationale: Wrong because norepinephrine acting on beta two receptors causes bronchodilation rather than constriction.

options.text: Acetylcholine blockade of muscarinic receptors causing dilation
options.rationale: Wrong because blockade of muscarinic receptors would reduce bronchoconstriction and produce dilation, not constriction.

options.text: Surfactant increase lowering surface tension causing dilation
options.rationale: Wrong because increased surfactant reduces surface tension and does not directly cause bronchoconstriction.

options.text: Nitric oxide mediated vasodilation of pulmonary vessels
options.rationale: Wrong because nitric oxide affects vascular tone and causes vasodilation, not bronchoconstriction of airways.

question: A 32-year-old with asthma receives a short-acting inhaled agent. Which receptor is the therapeutic target?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Beta two adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states beta two receptor activation causes bronchodilation and is the target for acute asthma therapy.

options.text: M three muscarinic receptors causing bronchodilation when activated
options.rationale: Wrong because M3 muscarinic receptor activation causes bronchoconstriction; blocking M3 would produce bronchodilation.

options.text: Alpha one adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle cells
options.rationale: Wrong because alpha one receptors are not the primary bronchodilatory target described in the lecture; beta two receptors mediate bronchodilation.

options.text: Dopamine D two receptors modulating airway secretions and tone
options.rationale: Wrong because dopamine D2 receptors are not described in the lecture as mediators of bronchial smooth muscle tone or bronchodilator therapy.

options.text: Histamine H one receptors causing bronchodilation when blocked
options.rationale: Wrong because H1 receptor blockade reduces histamine-mediated bronchoconstriction but the primary acute bronchodilator target in asthma is beta two receptors.

question: Which physiologic variable is the main driver of ventilation under normal conditions?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the main mechanisms of respiratory regulation (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Central chemoreceptor response to changes in arterial CO2
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture identifies central chemoreceptors responding to CO2 as the primary ventilatory drive under normal conditions.

options.text: Peripheral chemoreceptor response to small oxygen changes
options.rationale: Wrong because peripheral chemoreceptors respond to hypoxia but only when PaO2 falls below approximately 65 mm Hg and are not the main normal drive.

options.text: Baroreceptor reflex changes in systemic arterial pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because baroreceptors modulate cardiovascular responses and are not the principal regulators of minute ventilation described in the lecture.

options.text: Pulmonary stretch receptor signaling during quiet breathing
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary stretch receptors influence breathing patterns but are not the main drive for ventilation under normal conditions.

options.text: Hypothalamic temperature sensing altering respiratory rate
options.rationale: Wrong because temperature can modulate respiration but is not the primary ventilatory drive identified in the lecture.

question: Which change increases the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient indicating lung disease?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the factors regulating O2 and CO2 alveolar pressures (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increase in PAO2 minus PaO2 difference from venous admixture
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines the A-a gradient as PAO2 minus PaO2 and an increased gradient indicates impaired gas exchange due to venous admixture or diffusion defects.

options.text: Decrease in inspired oxygen fraction with unchanged ventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because lowering inspired oxygen reduces PAO2 and PaO2 proportionally and does not necessarily increase the A-a gradient due to intrinsic lung disease.

options.text: Increase in alveolar ventilation lowering both CO2 and oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because increased ventilation lowers PACO2 and can raise PAO2, but this does not by itself indicate an increased A-a gradient from lung disease.

options.text: Decrease in cardiac output reducing pulmonary perfusion uniformly
options.rationale: Wrong because reduced perfusion can lower PaO2 but does not typically increase the A-a gradient in the same way as diffusion or shunt abnormalities.

options.text: Increase in hemoglobin concentration altering oxygen content
options.rationale: Wrong because hemoglobin concentration affects oxygen content but not the partial pressure difference between alveolar gas and arterial blood that defines the A-a gradient.

question: Which physical factor described in the lecture most increases airway radius and lowers resistance?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increased radial traction from surrounding lung parenchyma
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that radial traction from parenchymal 'cords' increases airway radius and reduces resistance.

options.text: Loss of parenchymal attachments as in emphysema
options.rationale: Wrong because loss of parenchymal attachments decreases radial traction and promotes airway collapse, increasing resistance rather than lowering it.

options.text: Enhanced parasympathetic vagal tone causing bronchoconstriction
options.rationale: Wrong because parasympathetic activation causes bronchoconstriction and reduces radius, increasing resistance.

options.text: Increased mucus clearance reducing airway lumen diameter
options.rationale: Wrong because increased mucus within the lumen would narrow the airway and increase resistance rather than increase radius.

options.text: Thickening of airway smooth muscle increasing lumen size
options.rationale: Wrong because smooth muscle thickening tends to narrow the lumen and increase resistance rather than enlarge it.

question: A patient with restrictive lung disease demonstrates rapid shallow breathing. Which work component is increased?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the factors affection the work of breathing (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Elastic work of breathing increased due to stiff lungs
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states fibrosis increases elastic work, favoring rapid shallow breaths to minimize elastic load.

options.text: Resistive work increased due to airway obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because resistive work is primarily increased in obstructive diseases like COPD, not in restrictive fibrosis.

options.text: Work of breathing decreased due to improved compliance
options.rationale: Wrong because restrictive disease decreases compliance and increases elastic work rather than decreasing work.

options.text: Metabolic work decreased causing lower ventilation demand
options.rationale: Wrong because metabolic work is unrelated to the mechanical elastic load described in restrictive lung disease.

options.text: Chest wall resistive work increased from pleural effusion
options.rationale: Wrong because while chest wall factors can affect work, the lecture specifically attributes rapid shallow breathing in fibrosis to increased elastic work.

question: Which clinical finding from the lecture best explains increased FEV1/FVC ratio in restrictive disease?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the types of compliance depending on the lung diseases (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Reduced total lung capacity with rapid early expiration
options.rationale: Correct because restrictive disease reduces lung volumes so a relatively preserved early expiratory flow yields an increased FEV1/FVC ratio as described in the lecture.

options.text: Marked airway obstruction causing prolonged expiration
options.rationale: Wrong because prolonged expiration and reduced FEV1/FVC ratio characterize obstructive disease, not restrictive disease.

options.text: Upper airway stenosis flattening expiratory limb
options.rationale: Wrong because upper airway stenosis alters loop shape but does not explain the increased FEV1/FVC ratio seen in restrictive disease.

options.text: Increased residual volume with hyperinflation
options.rationale: Wrong because increased residual volume and hyperinflation are features of obstructive disease and would lower rather than raise the FEV1/FVC ratio.

options.text: Loss of surfactant causing alveolar collapse during inspiration
options.rationale: Wrong because surfactant deficiency reduces compliance and causes atelectasis but does not explain the characteristic increased FEV1/FVC ratio of restrictive disease.

question: Which statement best describes Henry's law application to pulmonary gases?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the factors regulating O2 and CO2 alveolar pressures (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Dissolved gas partial pressure equals gas phase partial pressure
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that at equilibrium the partial pressure of dissolved gas in liquid equals the gas phase partial pressure though concentrations differ due to binding.

options.text: Bound gas molecules always determine dissolved gas partial pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because bound gas does not contribute to partial pressure; only dissolved gas molecules determine partial pressure per the lecture.

options.text: Chemically modified gas increases the measured partial pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because chemically modified forms like bicarbonate do not contribute to the gas partial pressure according to the lecture.

options.text: Solubility coefficient decreases dissolved concentration at equilibrium
options.rationale: Wrong because a higher solvent/gas partition coefficient increases dissolved concentration; a decrease would not be the general rule described.

options.text: Total gas partial pressure equals sum of bound and dissolved pressures
options.rationale: Wrong because bound gas does not contribute to partial pressure; partial pressure is determined by dissolved gas only as taught in the lecture.

question: A newborn delivered at 32 weeks lacks lamellar bodies on electron microscopy. Which immediate pathophysiology is expected?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the lung volumes and capacities (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increased alveolar surface tension causing collapse
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture links decreased lamellar bodies to surfactant deficiency which raises surface tension and predisposes to alveolar collapse.

options.text: Protease mediated destruction of alveolar septa
options.rationale: Wrong because protease mediated septal destruction is characteristic of emphysema and not the immediate consequence of surfactant deficiency in premature infants.

options.text: Excessive mucus plugging of small airways causing obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because mucus hypersecretion is associated with chronic smoking and bronchitis, not lamellar body deficiency in premature neonates.

options.text: Primary pulmonary arterial vasospasm causing hypoxemia
options.rationale: Wrong because while pulmonary vascular changes can occur, the direct result of absent lamellar bodies is surfactant deficiency leading to alveolar collapse rather than primary vasospasm.

options.text: Increased bronchial smooth muscle contractility causing wheeze
options.rationale: Wrong because increased bronchial smooth muscle contractility is typical of asthma and is not the direct effect of absent lamellar bodies in the neonate.

question: Which arterial blood gas pattern indicates alveolar hyperventilation per the lecture thresholds?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the factors regulating O2 and CO2 alveolar pressures (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: End tidal PCO2 less than thirty five millimeters mercury
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines end tidal PCO2 below 35 mm Hg as hyperventilation.

options.text: End tidal PCO2 greater than forty five millimeters mercury
options.rationale: Wrong because a PCO2 above 45 mm Hg indicates hypoventilation rather than hyperventilation per the lecture.

options.text: Arterial PO2 of one hundred millimeters mercury with normal PCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because a normal arterial PO2 with normal PCO2 does not indicate hyperventilation according to the lecture thresholds.

options.text: End tidal PCO2 equal to forty millimeters mercury at rest
options.rationale: Wrong because a PCO2 of 40 mm Hg is considered normal and does not meet the lecture definition of hyperventilation.

options.text: Arterial pH of seven point thirty six with elevated PCO2
options.rationale: Wrong because an elevated PCO2 with near normal pH suggests chronic retention and not hyperventilation as defined in the lecture.

question: Which pulmonary function change is most typical in emphysema according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the types of compliance depending on the lung diseases (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Increased total lung capacity with markedly reduced FEV1
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes emphysema as producing hyperinflation with increased TLC and a large reduction in FEV1 leading to low FEV1/FVC.

options.text: Decreased total lung capacity with preserved FEV1 ratio
options.rationale: Wrong because decreased TLC with preserved or increased FEV1/FVC is characteristic of restrictive disease, not emphysema.

options.text: Normal lung volumes with isolated diffusion impairment
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema typically alters volumes and flows rather than presenting with entirely normal volumes.

options.text: Marked increase in FEV1 with reduced residual volume
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema reduces FEV1 and increases residual volume rather than increasing FEV1.

options.text: Fixed reduction in peak expiratory flow only
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema affects multiple spirometric measures including FEV1 and TLC, not only peak flow.

question: Which exam finding from the lecture explains drumstick shaped fingers in chronic interstitial fibrosis?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the types of compliance depending on the lung diseases (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Chronic hypoxemia stimulating digital clubbing development
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture associates chronic interstitial lung disease with hypoxemia and clubbing, which presents as drumstick shaped fingers.

options.text: Hypercapnia causing peripheral vasoconstriction and clubbing
options.rationale: Wrong because hypercapnia does not directly cause clubbing; chronic hypoxemia is the mechanism linked to clubbing in interstitial disease.

options.text: Surfactant deficiency producing distal phalangeal deformities
options.rationale: Wrong because surfactant deficiency affects alveoli in neonates and is not the cause of digital clubbing in adults with fibrosis.

options.text: Excessive mucus production leading to periosteal bone changes
options.rationale: Wrong because mucus hypersecretion is not the mechanism for clubbing; clubbing is related to chronic hypoxemia and vascular changes.

options.text: Pulmonary hypertension causing direct osteogenic stimulation of digits
options.rationale: Wrong because while pulmonary hypertension can accompany chronic lung disease, clubbing is more directly linked to chronic hypoxemia rather than pulmonary arterial pressure alone.

question: Which physiologic relationship explains why airway radius most strongly affects resistance?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes airway radius as the dominant determinant of resistance, consistent with the strong nonlinear dependence described.

options.text: Resistance varies directly with airway length and not radius
options.rationale: Wrong because while length affects resistance, the lecture highlights radius as the most influential factor, not length alone.

options.text: Resistance is independent of airway radius at high lung volumes
options.rationale: Wrong because radius continues to influence resistance across lung volumes; high lung volumes may increase radius but do not remove its effect.

options.text: Resistance depends only on gas viscosity changes with temperature
options.rationale: Wrong because gas viscosity has a minor role compared to airway radius in determining resistance as taught in the lecture.

options.text: Resistance is primarily determined by alveolar surface tension
options.rationale: Wrong because surface tension affects compliance and alveolar stability but airway resistance is dominated by airway radius.

question: Which exam-style vignette asks for the next best step consistent with lecture management principles for acute bronchospasm?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Administer inhaled beta two agonist to relieve bronchospasm
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture indicates beta two agonists activate bronchial beta two receptors causing bronchodilation and are first-line for acute bronchospasm.

options.text: Give intravenous beta one blocker to reduce heart rate
options.rationale: Wrong because beta one blockers would not relieve bronchospasm and could worsen bronchoconstriction; a beta two agonist is appropriate instead.

options.text: Provide high flow oxygen only without bronchodilator therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen alone does not address bronchoconstriction; bronchodilator therapy is required for acute relief per the lecture.

options.text: Administer inhaled muscarinic agonist to increase secretions
options.rationale: Wrong because muscarinic agonists cause bronchoconstriction and increased secretions; antimuscarinic agents would be bronchodilatory but are not the first-line acute step described.

options.text: Start systemic corticosteroids immediately for rapid bronchodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because corticosteroids reduce inflammation but do not provide the immediate bronchodilation needed as the first acute step; beta two agonists act faster.

question: Which arterial blood gas calculation from the lecture yields an A-a gradient of approximately sixteen millimeters mercury for a COPD patient at barometric pressure 769 mm Hg with PaO2 60 mm Hg and PaCO2 60 mm Hg?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the factors regulating O2 and CO2 alveolar pressures (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Use alveolar gas equation then subtract PaO2 to get sixteen
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture demonstrates calculating PAO2 using (Patm minus 47) times FIO2 minus PACO2 over R then subtracting PaO2 yields an A-a gradient of about 16 mm Hg in the example.

options.text: Assume PAO2 equals inspired oxygen partial pressure directly
options.rationale: Wrong because PAO2 must be calculated with the alveolar gas equation accounting for water vapor and PACO2; it is not simply the inspired oxygen partial pressure.

options.text: Calculate A-a gradient by adding PaCO2 to PaO2 values
options.rationale: Wrong because the A-a gradient is PAO2 minus PaO2, not a sum of PaCO2 and PaO2.

options.text: Use end tidal CO2 value without adjusting for respiratory quotient
options.rationale: Wrong because the alveolar gas equation requires dividing PACO2 by the respiratory quotient R; ignoring R yields incorrect PAO2 and A-a gradient.

options.text: Estimate A-a gradient as zero in chronic lung disease
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic lung disease typically increases the A-a gradient; it is not zero as this option suggests.

question: Which structural airway feature is present in bronchi but patchy in smaller airways per the lecture histology table?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the lung volumes and capacities (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Cartilage present in trachea and patchy in bronchi
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture histology table lists cartilage as present in the trachea and patchy in bronchi.

options.text: Cilia absent in bronchi and present only in alveoli
options.rationale: Wrong because cilia are present in trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles but absent in alveoli according to the lecture.

options.text: Smooth muscle absent throughout trachea and bronchi
options.rationale: Wrong because smooth muscle is present in trachea and bronchi; it is not absent as this option claims.

options.text: Type II pneumocytes abundant in bronchiolar epithelium
options.rationale: Wrong because type II pneumocytes are alveolar cells and are not described as abundant in bronchiolar epithelium in the lecture.

options.text: Alveolar macrophages form cartilage in small airways
options.rationale: Wrong because alveolar macrophages are immune cells and do not form cartilage; this contradicts the histologic descriptions in the lecture.

question: Which physiologic effect explains why emphysema patients favor slow deep breaths per the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Evaluate the factors affection the work of breathing (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Reduced elastic recoil lowers elastic work favoring deep breaths
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes emphysema reduces elastic recoil so elastic work is low and resistive work is high, favoring slow deep breaths to overcome resistance.

options.text: Increased elastic stiffness forces rapid shallow breathing pattern
options.rationale: Wrong because increased elastic stiffness is characteristic of restrictive disease and leads to rapid shallow breathing, not emphysema.

options.text: Enhanced mucociliary clearance reduces need for deep inspirations
options.rationale: Wrong because mucociliary clearance does not explain the breathing pattern preference in emphysema described in the lecture.

options.text: Central chemoreceptor hypersensitivity to oxygen levels
options.rationale: Wrong because central chemoreceptors respond primarily to CO2 and are not the mechanism driving slow deep breaths in emphysema per the lecture.

options.text: Increased surfactant production improving lung compliance
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema involves loss of elastic fibers rather than increased surfactant production; surfactant changes do not explain the described breathing pattern.

question: Which exam-style question from the lecture demonstrates squamous metaplasia due to chronic smoking?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the lung volumes and capacities (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Bronchial epithelium replaced by stratified squamous cells
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes tobacco smoke causing pseudostratified ciliated epithelium to change to stratified squamous epithelium, i.e., squamous metaplasia.

options.text: Alveolar hyaline membranes forming after surfactant loss
options.rationale: Wrong because hyaline membranes are associated with diffuse alveolar damage and neonatal RDS, not the squamous metaplasia from smoking described in the lecture.

options.text: Interstitial fibrosis producing drumstick shaped fingers
options.rationale: Wrong because while fibrosis can cause clubbing, the specific histologic change from smoking discussed in the lecture is squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium.

options.text: Alveolar wall destruction by proteases in smokers
options.rationale: Wrong because alveolar wall destruction describes emphysema which can be smoking-related but is distinct from the epithelial squamous metaplasia highlighted in the smoking vignette.

options.text: Excessive mucus gland hyperplasia without epithelial change
options.rationale: Wrong because smoking causes both mucus gland hyperplasia and epithelial metaplasia; the key exam vignette emphasized epithelial stratification change rather than isolated gland hyperplasia.

question: Which physiologic description from the lecture explains dynamic airway compression during forced expiration?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the forces acting on the lung and importance of dynamic airway compression (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Effort independent flow limited by intrathoracic airway collapse
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that during forced expiration airflow becomes effort independent due to dynamic airway compression determined by elastic recoil and airway resistance.

options.text: Peak expiratory flow increases linearly with effort always
options.rationale: Wrong because peak flow has an effort dependent portion but later becomes effort independent due to dynamic compression, so it does not increase linearly with effort throughout expiration.

options.text: Inspiration causes dynamic compression limiting inspiratory flow
options.rationale: Wrong because dynamic compression is a phenomenon of forced expiration when intrapleural pressures compress airways, not a limiting factor during normal inspiration.

options.text: Airflow solely determined by airway length during forced expiration
options.rationale: Wrong because airflow is influenced by elastic recoil and resistance, with radius being the dominant factor rather than airway length alone.

options.text: Effort independent flow reflects increased alveolar surfactant
options.rationale: Wrong because effort independent flow is due to mechanical compression and resistance, not changes in surfactant levels.

question: Which option best describes the contribution of dissolved oxygen to arterial PO2 and content?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the factors regulating O2 and CO2 alveolar pressures (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Dissolved oxygen determines PaO2 and is 0.003 times PO2
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states dissolved O2 creates PaO2 and its amount equals 0.003 times PO2 in mm Hg.

options.text: Bound oxygen determines PaO2 independently of dissolved fraction
options.rationale: Wrong because bound oxygen on hemoglobin does not contribute to partial pressure; PaO2 is set by dissolved oxygen.

options.text: Chemically modified oxygen increases PaO2 directly
options.rationale: Wrong because chemically modified forms like bicarbonate do not contribute to gas partial pressures such as PaO2.

options.text: Total oxygen content equals dissolved oxygen only
options.rationale: Wrong because total oxygen content includes both dissolved oxygen and oxygen bound to hemoglobin, not dissolved alone.

options.text: Hemoglobin saturation is independent of PaO2 values
options.rationale: Wrong because hemoglobin saturation depends on PaO2 as described by the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation relationship in the lecture.

question: Which exam vignette requires identifying the mechanism of increased pulmonary arterial pressure from generalized hypoxia?
cited_learning_objective: Define the category of hypoxic vasoconstriction (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Global alveolar hypoxia causing widespread precapillary vasoconstriction
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains generalized alveolar hypoxia triggers precapillary vasoconstriction throughout the lungs, raising pulmonary arterial pressure and causing pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: Local bronchial obstruction producing systemic vasodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because local bronchial obstruction causes regional hypoxic vasoconstriction to divert blood, not systemic vasodilation.

options.text: Left heart failure causing passive pulmonary venous hypertension
options.rationale: Wrong because left heart failure raises pulmonary venous pressure passively and is a different mechanism from hypoxic precapillary vasoconstriction described in the lecture.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism causing global hypoxic vasodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary embolism causes vascular obstruction and may increase pulmonary pressures but does not produce the hypoxic precapillary vasoconstriction mechanism emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Systemic hypoxia reducing pulmonary vascular resistance uniformly
options.rationale: Wrong because systemic hypoxia in the lungs causes vasoconstriction and increased pulmonary vascular resistance rather than reducing it.

question: Which option best matches the lecture explanation for why COPD can lead to right heart failure?
cited_learning_objective: Define the category of hypoxic vasoconstriction (AACOM I.2. b; II.1.f; III.3.a; OMED-620 – 1, 2, 12)

options.text: Chronic alveolar hypoxia causing pulmonary hypertension and RV strain
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture links chronic hypoxia to widespread hypoxic vasoconstriction, raising pulmonary arterial pressure and causing right ventricular hypertrophy and failure.

options.text: Left ventricular failure causing secondary pulmonary venous hypertension
options.rationale: Wrong because left ventricular failure causes pulmonary venous hypertension but the lecture specifically attributes COPD related right heart failure to hypoxic vasoconstriction.

options.text: Primary systemic hypertension transmitting pressure to pulmonary circuit
options.rationale: Wrong because systemic hypertension does not directly cause pulmonary hypertension via the mechanism described in COPD; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is the key factor.

options.text: Pulmonary emboli causing acute right ventricular overload only
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary emboli can cause acute RV strain but the chronic process in COPD leading to RV failure is due to hypoxic vasoconstriction and sustained pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: Excessive oxygen therapy causing pulmonary vasodilation and failure
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen therapy tends to reduce hypoxic vasoconstriction; it does not cause pulmonary hypertension leading to right heart failure as described in COPD.
